blocks.x: Winter can be a slow time to lease a rental in Winnipeg, which makes a unit turnover checklist worth having before the next move-out notice arrives. Rents have softened too: at $1,319, the average unfurnished one-bedroom asking rent in [liv.rent's October 2026 report](https://liv.rent/blog/?p=69631) was down three months in a row, though the latest drop was only 0.1%.
When renters have choices, units that are ready on day one have an edge. This checklist covers the property management renovations to plan between November and March.
Before the resident moves out

**Walk the unit early, ideally 30 to 60 days before move-out.** Note damage and wear so you can order materials early. Manitoba [limits when a landlord can enter](https://www.gov.mb.ca/cca/rtb/resource_list/privacy.pdf), so get the tenant's agreement first, or give written notice where the rules allow it. The Residential Tenancies Branch can explain what applies.
**Book trades now.** Painters, flooring installers and repair crews can get busy before the holidays. Lock in dates before the notice period ends.
**Order long-lead items.** Appliances, windows, doors and custom counters can be slow to arrive in winter, so order them early.
The winter unit turnover checklist: what to renovate first

**1. Heat and drafts.** Prospects notice cold units instantly in a Winnipeg January. Have a heating contractor check furnace or boiler operation. Replace weatherstripping, fix door sweeps, and inspect windows for failed seals or frost buildup.
**2. Paint.** Fresh, neutral paint throughout. Use washable finishes in kitchens, bathrooms and hallways.

**3. Flooring.** Replace worn carpet with luxury vinyl plank. It handles salt, slush and boots better and can last through multiple turns. In older buildings, [test old tile and adhesive for asbestos](/blog/asbestos-testing-before-renovating-manitoba) before they come up.
**4. Kitchen and bath refresh.** New hardware, faucets, light fixtures, and re-caulked tubs and sinks make an older unit feel updated.
**5. Lighting.** Short winter days mean showings in low light. Replace dim bulbs, and have an electrician add fixtures where rooms feel dark.
**6. Safety items.** Last on this list, but never skip them: test smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, check railings and secure entry locks.
Common areas count too
Prospects judge the building before they see the unit. Before winter showings:
Keep entrances clear of snow and ice, and well lit.
Use durable entry mats and clean salt stains on lobby floors.
Repair damaged entry doors, mailboxes and hallway flooring.
Plan winter-friendly renovation work

Winter is a good time for **interior** property management renovations: [kitchens](/services/kitchen-renovations), [bathrooms](/services/bathroom-renovations), [flooring](/services/flooring) and paint, because the work is indoors and less affected by the cold. Save exterior work like masonry, painting and siding for the warmer months.
Keep the turn short
Set a target for a standard turn, counted from move-out to show-ready, and track each unit against it. Ways to get there:
Standardize finishes (one paint colour, one flooring, one fixture package) across units.
Keep a stock of common parts: hardware, faucets, outlets, blinds.
Schedule trades back-to-back, not one at a time.
Photograph and list the unit the day it's ready.
The bottom line
In winter, every vacant day counts. Property managers who plan turns before move-out, fix heat and drafts first, and standardize finishes give their units a better chance of leasing, even in January.
